title: How to Build Pseudorandom Unitaries in Microcrypt
abstract: We provide the first evidence relative to a classical oracle that pseudorandom unitaries (PRUs) can exist without quantum-computable one-way functions. To obtain this result, we first prove that five independent random diagonal phase layers interleaved with Hadamard transforms \[ U=F_5HF_4HF_3HF_2HF_1 \] form a strong PRU with security under adaptive, controlled access to the unitary, its inverse, transpose, and complex conjugate. Our main result is that, when the phase layers are implemented using a classical random oracle O, the construction remains secure against uniform BQP adversaries with coherent access to suitable Boolean completions of classical-input $QMA^{PH}^{O}}$ decision problems. Such an adversary can invert (even quantum-computable) one-way functions and solve efficiently verifiable one-way puzzles defined relative to O. Our result therefore provides classical-oracle evidence that PRUs do not imply quantum-computable one-way functions, in the form of a black-box separation. We substantially strengthen the classical-oracle result of Kretschmer, Qian, and Tal (STOC 2025) by obtaining PRUs secure against these QMA-aided adversaries. Our construction also consists of a simple, efficient circuit that queries a random function, suggesting a route to concrete implementation via the random-oracle heuristic.

bite.hook: Researchers provide the first classical-oracle evidence that pseudorandom unitaries can exist without one-way functions.
tldr: The researchers investigated whether pseudorandom unitaries can be built without relying on quantum-computable one-way functions.
They constructed a PRU using five random diagonal phase layers interleaved with Hadamard transforms and analyzed its security.
Their results show security against advanced adversaries that can invert one-way functions, providing a black-box separation.
bite.whyItMatters: One-way functions are a cornerstone of modern cryptography. Proving that certain advanced cryptographic tools can exist independently of them reshapes our foundational understanding of computational security in a quantum world.
bite.eli5: Think of a cryptographic lockbox. Scientists just showed it's possible to build an unbreakable high-tech vault even if a specific kind of elementary math puzzle (a one-way function) turns out to be solvable.

glossary.shortDef: Quantum operations that look completely random to any efficient observer, but are generated deterministically.
glossary.eli5Def: A secret shuffling machine that mixes up quantum states so thoroughly that nobody can tell it apart from pure randomness.

glossary.shortDef: Functions that are easy to compute in one direction, but hard to invert.
glossary.eli5Def: Like cracking an egg: super easy to do, but virtually impossible to put back together.

glossary.shortDef: A quantum gate that creates superposition by mapping basis states to equal linear combinations.
glossary.eli5Def: A quantum coin-flip that puts a bit into a state of spinning between both heads and tails at once.

glossary.shortDef: A theoretical black box that can instantly solve specific computational problems.
glossary.eli5Def: A magical helper box that instantly answers certain hard questions whenever you ask it.
